questions.question: A hardwood forest holds sugar maples, American beeches and yellow birches, with deer, ferns and mushrooms living among them. Which group from this forest is a population?
questions.answer: Every sugar maple growing in it
choices: Every sugar maple growing in it
Every tree of any kind growing in it
Every sugar maple and beech in it
One sugar maple and its own seedlings
questions.context: A population is all the members of one species living in one area, so the forest's sugar maples, young and old, make up one population. Trees of every kind, or maples and beeches together, are several populations living side by side, and one tree with its seedlings is only a few members of its population.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.12C asks 6th graders to describe the levels from organism to community, and one species against many is the line that marks out a population.

questions.question: Each spring the bullfrogs of a pond lay their eggs in its shallow water, and the tadpoles that hatch take one to three years to become frogs. An ecologist sets out to count the pond's bullfrog population. Should she count the tadpoles?
questions.answer: Yes, since young bullfrogs belong to it too
choices: Yes, since young bullfrogs belong to it too
Yes, but only once they have grown legs
No, since tadpoles are too young to breed
No, since tadpoles breathe with gills, like fish
questions.context: A population is every member of one species in an area, of every age, so the tadpoles count with the grown frogs, legs or no legs; ecologists even track how many are at each stage of life. A tadpole breathes with gills, but it is a young frog, not a fish, and the same species as its parents.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn that a population is all the members of one species in an area, and counting the young is the plainest test of 'all'.

questions.question: In the levels of ecological organisation, a community sits one level above a population. What makes the community the higher level?
questions.answer: It is made up of many populations
choices: It is made up of many populations
It is one part of a larger population
It adds the water, mud and rocks
It holds more members of a single species
questions.context: A community is all the populations of different species living together in one area, so it holds a population and more besides, as a pond holds its bullfrogs, sunfish, cattails and algae. The water, mud and rocks join in only at the next level up, the ecosystem.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.12C asks 6th graders to describe the hierarchy of organism, population and community, which rests on each level holding the one below it.

questions.question: Ecologists can describe a pond as a community or as an ecosystem. Which belongs to the pond's ecosystem but not to its community?
choices: The sunlight warming its water
The bacteria living in its mud
The algae floating on its surface
The cattails growing along its edge
questions.context: A community is the living things alone, and an ecosystem is the community together with its nonliving surroundings, so sunlight, like the water and the mud, joins only in the ecosystem. The bacteria in the mud and the algae are tiny, but they are alive, so they belong to both.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn that an ecosystem is the community plus its nonliving surroundings, the line students most often blur (TEKS 6.12C).

questions.question: Life on Earth reaches from microbes drifting about 10 kilometres up in the air to the floor of the deepest ocean trench, nearly 11 kilometres down. All of Earth's ecosystems together form the highest level of ecological organisation. What is it called?
choices: The biosphere
The atmosphere
The hydrosphere
The geosphere
questions.context: The biosphere is every ecosystem on Earth, the whole zone where life is found. The atmosphere is the air around Earth, the hydrosphere all its water and the geosphere its solid ground, and living things reach into parts of each of them.
questions.grade_note: Texas's older 6th-grade standard ran the levels of organisation on to the biosphere, the top level, and Earth's spheres are taught beside it.

questions.question: Every ecosystem on Earth, from a pond to an ocean, belongs to one great whole, the top level of ecological organisation. Scientists know of no other planet or moon with ecosystems of its own. Why not?
questions.answer: No other world is known to have life
choices: No other world is known to have life
No other world is known to have water
No other world is known to have an atmosphere
No other world is known to have clouds
questions.context: Every ecosystem is built on a community of living things, so it is life that no other world is known to have. Mars has water ice at its poles, and Mars and Venus both have atmospheres, Venus wrapped in thick clouds, yet no life has been found on either, or anywhere beyond Earth.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn that the biosphere is all of Earth's ecosystems, and that Earth is the only world known to hold life.

questions.question: In one forest, the trees draw nitrogen, a nutrient, up from the soil through their roots and drop it again in their fallen leaves. Fungi and bacteria rot the leaves and return the nitrogen to the soil. Which level of organisation does an ecologist study when she follows this loop?
choices: The ecosystem
The community
The population
The biosphere
questions.context: The loop runs between living things, the trees, fungi and bacteria, and a nonliving part, the soil, so it belongs to the ecosystem, the community together with its surroundings. A study of the trees, fungi and bacteria alone would stop at the community, and the biosphere is all of Earth's ecosystems, not one forest.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn that an ecosystem joins a community to its nonliving surroundings, and a nutrient passing between soil and living things is the plainest case.

questions.question: A small town is home to people, dogs, pigeons, oak trees, lawns and the bacteria in its soil, among its roads and houses. To an ecologist, where do the town's people belong in its levels of organisation?
questions.answer: In its community, as one population
choices: In its community, as one population
In its ecosystem, but not its community
Outside its ecosystem, apart from nature
In a separate community of their own
questions.context: People are living things of one species, so the town's people are a population, and with the dogs, pigeons, trees, grass and bacteria they make up the town's community; the roads, houses and soil join them in its ecosystem. Everyday speech calls a town's people its community, but to an ecologist one species alone is never a community.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders sort real cases into the levels of organisation, and teachers report that students leave people out of ecosystems.

questions.question: Under one rotting log, in about a square foot of forest floor, live beetles, ants, pill bugs, fungi and a salamander. Across many kilometres of the same forest, an ecologist counts the eastern gray squirrels. Which of the two groups sits at the higher level of organisation?
questions.answer: The log's group, since it holds many species
choices: The log's group, since it holds many species
The squirrels, since they cover far more ground
The squirrels, since each is a larger animal
Neither, since each group is one population
questions.context: The life under the log is a community, populations of several species living together, however small the patch. The squirrels, spread over far more ground, are still one species and so one population, for a step up the levels adds more kinds of living things, not more land.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.12C has 6th graders order organism, population and community, and teachers stress that each step up adds kinds of living things, not area.
